title: Waltzes and sweet bands like Wayne King
summary: Territory bands played stock waltzes for dances; Smith describes Wayne King and Guy Lombardo and how the band felt playing sweet repertory.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: So, when a band like the Blue Devils or Eddie and Sugar Lou or Eli Rice or any one of these little bands that was going around...
When they went around to do gigs in dance halls, would they be expected to play waltzes and all that kind of stuff?
And presumably, these would not be numbers where people would improvise much. You'd simply play from a stock.

Yeah. They had most of the waltzes that they got from stocks. Because they were writing a lot of waltzes in those stocks during them days. Because Guy Lombardo and bands like those, and them hotel bands, they played a lot of waltzes. And we'd get some of them jobs where they couldn't make it, and that
owner wanted us to play some of the waltzes, too. Yeah, Wade King. He was the one famous horn who come down through this way, playing all those fine waltzes and stuff.
No. He was a White band. Wade King, yeah. He played all that beautiful straight alto. Never did play no solo. Nothing but just straight lead. He had a solo, but it was straight lead.
Would the Blue Devils ever do gigs where you were expected to play like that all night?
For instance, would you ever play gigs just for White people?

Yeah. Illinois. You stayed in Illinois...you'd go up there, and if you didn't play like Wayne King, Guy Lombardo and this other band that played that kind of music... [JAN GARBER] Your repertory had to sound like that on (?) . Sweet stuff.
What did the guys in the band feel about doing gigs like that?

Oh, it was all right. They said, 'Well, we just ain't got the repertory to keep up with this. Be glad when this night's over with, and we go back where we can get in the (?) or something like that.' They'd put it that way.
